terms.comment: Lewis & Short cite it of waking from sleep only from Suetonius and the Vulgate; Cicero and Livy say excitō.

evidence: Cic. Rep. 6.12: nē mē ē somnō excitētis (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 39, 403: wake up, tr., (ē somnō) excitāre
terms.comment: The usual verb of classical prose, often with ē somnō.

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.44: aliquem ē somnō (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: Suscitā istum, Delphium. — Callidamatēs, Callidamatēs, vigilā.
phrases.english: Wake him up, Delphium. — Callidamates, Callidamates, wake up!

phrases.latin: tantō silentiō in summum ēvāsēre ut nōn custōdēs sōlum fallerent, sed nē canēs quidem, sollicitum animal ad nocturnōs strepitūs, excitārent
phrases.english: they reached the top so quietly that they slipped past the guards and did not even wake the dogs, creatures that fret at every noise in the night

phrases.latin: hī nostrī vigilēs nocturnī, quōs excitandīs in opera mortālibus rumpendōque somnō nātūra genuit
phrases.english: these night watchmen of ours, whom nature made to wake us mortals for our work and break our sleep

sources: Lewis & Short: excito · Lewis & Short: suscito
